texts.label: A
texts.title: The coastal survey
texts.text: Our team spent seven days recording shorebird behaviour on a windy estuary. The most useful change was methodological: we replaced a fixed timetable with observations triggered by the tide. That produced fewer neat comparisons but captured feeding periods we had previously missed. The revised schedule changed the team’s argument about accuracy. A neat timetable had looked scientific because it was easy to compare, but it missed when birds actually fed. The better record was less tidy and more faithful. The experience changed the writer’s interpretation of the task, not merely the amount of information available. That distinction is what makes the account useful beyond its immediate setting. The writer’s conclusion remains qualified. It values the change because it altered attention and behaviour, while acknowledging that no single method works independently of context, time and human judgement. The account is persuasive because the writer describes a change in method, not simply a successful result. Readers can compare the original expectation with the later interpretation and see why the experience mattered. This careful qualification gives the reader a transferable lesson rather than a simple recommendation.

texts.label: B
texts.title: The night insects
texts.text: At first I thought the difficulty would be identifying species in darkness. In fact, it was remaining still beside the light trap while moths arrived. The work was repetitive, yet the repetition made tiny differences in flight and colour easier to notice. The field notes became a record of attention as much as identification. Patience meant creating conditions in which a difference could become evidence rather than noise. texts.label: C
texts.title: The mountain plants
texts.text: The altitude was less demanding than the weather. A sudden snowfall forced us to abandon one site and return two days later. The interruption was frustrating, but it revealed how quickly the plants’ open flowers closed in response to cold. Returning to the site allowed comparison of an expected seasonal pattern with an immediate response to cold. Weather was part of the habitat, not background. texts.label: D
texts.title: The urban foxes
texts.text: Residents had strong opinions about the foxes before we began. Rather than asking whether foxes were liked or disliked, we mapped where encounters occurred and when bins were left outside. The resulting discussion was calmer because it began with shared observations. The maps did not settle the dispute, but moved it from a general argument to precise questions about timing, access and responsibility. questions.prompt: Which fieldwork involved changing the schedule in response to natural conditions?
questions.explanation: The coastal team replaced a fixed timetable with tide-triggered observations.

questions.prompt: Which fieldwork made a researcher appreciate the value of repetition?
questions.explanation: Repetition made small differences easier to notice.

questions.prompt: Which fieldwork was interrupted but produced an unexpected insight?
questions.explanation: The snowfall caused a return visit that revealed the plants’ response to cold.

questions.prompt: Which fieldwork changed the tone of a local conversation?
questions.explanation: Shared mapping observations made the discussion calmer.

questions.prompt: Which researcher had expected a different practical difficulty?
questions.explanation: The writer expected identification to be difficult but found remaining still was the challenge.

questions.prompt: Which team found that less tidy data could be more informative?
questions.explanation: The team accepted fewer neat comparisons in order to capture missed feeding periods.

questions.prompt: Which account describes returning to a location?
questions.explanation: The team returned two days after abandoning a site.

questions.prompt: Which account says the research began by measuring events rather than opinions?
questions.explanation: The researchers mapped encounters and bin timing instead of asking for preferences.

questions.prompt: Which account focuses on noticing variation within a group of similar subjects?
questions.explanation: The repetition made differences among moths easier to notice.

questions.prompt: Which account suggests that environmental responsiveness was itself significant?
questions.explanation: The plants’ rapid response to cold became the unexpected finding.
